processing: Fully oxidised Ceylon black tea, made in the factory Thomas Lipton had built in 1890 and which still operates.
harvest_season: Year-round. Teas from the Uva side are generally most prized from the dry season in the middle of the year.
appearance_dry: Dark broken leaf, as is usual for Ceylon factory grades.
appearance_liquor: Bright coppery red, as is typical of Uva-side teas.
taste_profile: Notes on this estate's own tea are few. As with other high teas on the Uva side, expect a brisk and bright cup.

brewing.notes: Western style. Fine with milk; broken grades need only about three minutes.

vintage_note: Sold by grade and through the trade, not by vintage. Drink within a year or two. Dry-season lots are the ones to ask for, as with other teas from the Uva side.
description:
Dambatenne is the estate above Haputale forever tied to Thomas Lipton: his first tea plantation on the island and the home of a factory called the longest in Sri Lanka, at about 1,566 m above sea level. Lipton's Seat, the famous viewpoint, sits on the hills above it.

It is a working estate making black tea in the ordinary Ceylon way, in a factory you can visit. The old building is much of the draw.

Published tasting notes are few. As with other teas on the Uva side, expect something brisk and bright; brew it short and try it both black and with milk.

When you buy it, look for the grade and date; the Lipton story adds nothing to the cup.
history:
Thomas Lipton bought the estate in the late 19th century, and the factory dates from 1890. Figures for the size vary, from 2,500 acres in one account to 873 hectares in another.

Lipton kept the estate for about four decades. One account says estate and factory changed hands in 1930.
